Empirical studies show corporate tax cuts primarily benefit shareholders via stock buybacks and dividends, not workers. A 2019 NBER analysis found increased corporate taxes raised wages by 60% of the cost burden, meaning workers bore most of the cost of lower rates.

Job growth is driven by consumer demand, labor market conditions, and business confidence—not tax policy focused on balance sheets. When companies receive tax windfalls, they rarely expand payrolls proportionally. The 2017 US tax cuts illustrate this: stock buybacks surged to $850 billion while job growth gains were marginal and short-lived.

Long-term employment depends on investment in skills, infrastructure, and demand-side policies that put money in workers' pockets who then spend it—creating a jobs multiplier effect. Top-down tax cuts lack this mechanism. Research by Congressional Budget Office and economists across the political spectrum consistently find that corporate tax reductions have minimal, if any, significant impact on employment levels over time.
